summary: This work reframes superconducting qubit readout optimization from maximizing single-shot fidelity to minimizing wall-clock certification time by treating dispersive measurement as a stochastic communication channel governed by classical Chernoff information. For transmon parameters with $\chi/2\pi = 1.2$ MHz, $\kappa/2\pi = 5.0$ MHz, $n̄ = 80$, $\eta = 0.45$, and $T_1 = 30$ µs, the throughput-optimal integration time $\tau_\mathrm{rate} \approx 1.22$ µs exceeds the fidelity-optimal time $\tau_\mathrm{fid} \approx 0.78$ µs, yielding 9–11% certification speedups that saturate at 1.13× in high-power, high-overhead regimes.
motivation: Single-shot fidelity optimization does not minimize total certification time in high-throughput processors because it ignores the amortization of fixed per-shot hardware overheads ($\tau_\mathrm{oh} \sim 15$ µs) across multiple measurement shots.
method: A trajectory model with full cavity memory incorporating stochastic $T_1$ relaxation computes classical Chernoff information $C(\tau)$ from matched-filter score distributions; total certification time $T_\mathrm{cert}(\tau) = [\log(1/\epsilon)/C(\tau)](\tau + \tau_\mathrm{oh})$ is then numerically minimized. An information-extraction efficiency metric $\eta_\mathrm{info}(\tau) = C(\tau)/C_\mathrm{ideal}(\tau)$ benchmarks performance against a unit-efficiency Gaussian limit.
result: Information-extraction efficiency reaches ~45% at short integration times but drops to $\eta_\mathrm{info}(1.22 \text{ µs}) \approx 0.12$ at the throughput-optimal point due to $T_1$-induced trajectory smearing; this systematic separation between $\tau_\mathrm{fid}$ and $\tau_\mathrm{rate}$ persists even in the $T_1 \to \infty$ limit, proving it is a structural consequence of non-zero overhead rather than decoherence alone.
